chunks.title: VoltNest 13 Owner's Guide
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: The VoltNest 13 is a wall-mounted home battery that stores energy from your rooftop solar or the grid and powers your home when you need it. It holds 13.5 kWh of usable energy and can charge or discharge at up to 5.0 kW continuously, which is enough to run most of a typical home at once. Each home has one VoltNest 13, installed next to the main electrical panel. The battery works on its own once it is set up: it decides when to charge and discharge based on the operating mode and reserve percentage you choose in the app.

chunks.title: VoltNest 13 Owner's Guide
chunks.heading: Reserve percentage
chunks.text: The reserve percentage is the share of the VoltNest 13's charge that it keeps back for power outages. During normal days, the battery will not discharge below this level to save you money; that energy waits for the moment the grid goes down. The default reserve is 20%, or about 2.7 kWh of the 13.5 kWh capacity. You can change it in the app from 10% to 100% in steps of 5%. A higher reserve gives you more backup during an outage but leaves less energy for avoiding peak prices. A lower reserve saves more money day to day but gives you less protection.

chunks.title: VoltNest 13 Owner's Guide
chunks.heading: Operating modes
chunks.text: The VoltNest 13 has three operating modes. Self-Powered stores extra solar during the day and uses it to power your home in the evening and overnight. Time-Based Control follows your electricity plan: it avoids buying power during peak hours and can charge from the grid when prices are lowest. Backup Only keeps the battery full and saves all of its energy for outages. You can switch modes at any time in the app. Grid charging is only allowed in Time-Based Control.

chunks.title: VoltNest 13 Owner's Guide
chunks.heading: Reading the status screen
chunks.text: The VoltNest 13 status screen shows three things. State of charge is the percentage of the 13.5 kWh capacity currently stored; 50% means about 6.75 kWh. Power is how fast energy is flowing right now, in kW: a battery discharging at 1.2 kW is supplying 1.2 kWh to your home every hour. The status label tells you whether the battery is charging, discharging, or idle. Power and stored energy are different: power is the rate, stored energy is the amount left.

chunks.title: VoltNest 13 Owner's Guide
chunks.heading: Charging from the grid
chunks.text: In Time-Based Control mode, the VoltNest 13 can charge from the grid during your plan's cheapest hours. It charges at up to 5.0 kW, so going from empty to full takes about 2.7 hours. Some energy is lost in every charge and discharge: round-trip efficiency is about 90%, so storing 1 kWh from the grid gives you about 0.9 kWh back later. Grid charging pays off when the price difference between cheap and peak hours is larger than that 10% loss, and when your solar forecast is too low to fill the battery on its own.

chunks.title: VoltNest 13 Owner's Guide
chunks.heading: Care and safety
chunks.text: The VoltNest 13 needs no routine maintenance. Keep the vents clear and do not stack items against the unit. Never open the battery case or the electrical panel it connects to. Installation, wiring changes, moving the battery, and repairs must be done by a licensed electrician. If the status screen shows a fault, or you notice heat, smoke, or a burning smell, turn the battery off in the app, keep people away from the unit, and call a licensed electrician or emergency services.

chunks.title: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.heading: Should I charge my battery from the grid tonight?
chunks.text: Whether to charge your battery from the grid tonight depends on tomorrow's solar forecast and how much charge the battery has now. Charging between 12 AM and 6 AM costs $0.11 per kWh. After charging losses (round-trip efficiency is 90% for a VoltNest 13 and 88% for a Helio PowerCell 10), each usable kWh costs about $0.12 to $0.13, compared with $0.48 per kWh if you buy power during the 4 PM to 9 PM peak. If tomorrow looks cloudy and the battery is low, charging overnight is usually worth it. If tomorrow looks sunny, solar will refill the battery and grid charging is usually unnecessary.

chunks.title: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.heading: When is electricity cheapest?
chunks.text: On the Brightline Energy Sunrise Saver plan, electricity is cheapest between 12 AM and 6 AM, at $0.11 per kWh. This super off-peak period is the same every day of the year, including weekends and holidays. The most expensive time is 4 PM to 9 PM, at $0.48 per kWh. All other hours are off-peak, at $0.24 per kWh.

chunks.title: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.heading: What does state of charge mean?
chunks.text: State of charge is how full your battery is, as a percentage of its capacity: 13.5 kWh for a VoltNest 13 and 10 kWh for a Helio PowerCell 10. A VoltNest 13 at 50% holds about 6.75 kWh; a Helio PowerCell 10 at 50% holds 5 kWh. State of charge tells you how much energy is stored, not how fast it is being used; that rate is the power, shown in kW.

chunks.title: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.heading: Why is my battery discharging during the day?
chunks.text: Your battery discharges whenever your home is using more power than your rooftop solar is producing. This is normal in everyday modes such as Self-Powered on a VoltNest 13 or Solar First on a Helio PowerCell 10. It often happens on cloudy days, early in the morning before solar ramps up, and when large appliances such as air conditioning run at midday. The battery will not discharge below your reserve percentage except during a power outage.

chunks.title: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.heading: Can I add another battery or new circuits?
chunks.text: Adding a second battery, adding new circuits, or changing which circuits the battery backs up all require work inside the electrical panel. This work must be done by a licensed electrician, who can check that your panel and wiring can safely handle the change. Do not attempt any wiring or panel work yourself.

chunks.title: Frequently Asked Questions
chunks.heading: Is my data shared?
chunks.text: This assistant only uses the demo battery, rate plan, and solar data built into it. It does not connect to a real battery or utility account, and it does not store your messages after you close the page. Please avoid typing personal information into the chat.

chunks.title: Helio PowerCell 10 User Manual
chunks.heading: Overview
chunks.text: The Helio PowerCell 10 from Helio Systems is a compact home battery that stores energy from your rooftop solar or the grid and powers your home when you need it. It holds 10 kWh of usable energy and can charge or discharge at up to 3.8 kW continuously, which covers lighting, the refrigerator, and most everyday appliances at once, but not several large loads together. The Helio PowerCell 10 mounts indoors or in a garage and is managed from the Helio app, where you choose its operating mode and reserve percentage.

chunks.title: Helio PowerCell 10 User Manual
chunks.heading: Reserve percentage
chunks.text: The reserve percentage is the share of the Helio PowerCell 10's charge kept back for power outages. On normal days the battery will not discharge below this level; that energy waits for the grid to go down. The default reserve is 15%, or 1.5 kWh of the 10 kWh capacity, and you can change it in the Helio app from 10% to 100% in steps of 5%. The Helio PowerCell 10 also keeps a fixed 10% backup floor it never goes below, even in an outage, to protect the cells. A higher reserve means more backup and less energy for avoiding peak prices.

chunks.title: Helio PowerCell 10 User Manual
chunks.heading: Operating modes
chunks.text: The Helio PowerCell 10 has three operating modes. Solar First stores extra solar during the day and uses it to power your home in the evening, keeping grid use as low as possible. Cost Saver follows your electricity plan: it avoids buying power during peak hours and can charge from the grid when prices are lowest. Storm Guard keeps the battery full and saves all of its energy for outages. You can switch modes at any time in the Helio app. Grid charging is only allowed in Cost Saver mode.

chunks.title: Helio PowerCell 10 User Manual
chunks.heading: Reading the status display
chunks.text: The Helio PowerCell 10 status display shows the state of charge as a percentage of its 10 kWh capacity, so 50% means 5 kWh stored. It also shows power flow in kW, with an arrow pointing in when the battery is charging and out when it is discharging, and a leaf icon when the battery is running on solar alone. Power is the rate energy is moving right now; stored energy is how much is left.

chunks.title: Helio PowerCell 10 User Manual
chunks.heading: Charging from the grid
chunks.text: In Cost Saver mode, the Helio PowerCell 10 can charge from the grid during your plan's cheapest hours. It charges at up to 3.8 kW, so going from the 10% floor to full takes about 2.4 hours. Round-trip efficiency is about 88%: storing 1 kWh from the grid gives you about 0.88 kWh back later. Grid charging pays off when the gap between cheap and peak prices is bigger than that 12% loss and your solar forecast is too low to fill the battery on its own.

chunks.title: Helio PowerCell 10 User Manual
chunks.heading: Care and safety
chunks.text: The Helio PowerCell 10 needs no routine maintenance, but keep at least 15 cm of clear space around its vents and keep it out of direct sun. Never open the battery case or the electrical panel it connects to. Installation, moving the battery, wiring changes, and repairs must be done by a licensed electrician. If the status display shows a red fault light, or you notice heat, smoke, or a burning smell, switch the battery off in the Helio app, keep people away, and call a licensed electrician or emergency services.

chunks.title: Backup Power During Outages
chunks.heading: What happens when the grid goes down
chunks.text: When the grid goes down, your home battery switches your home to backup power automatically, in less than a second. Most people never notice the switch: lights stay on and devices keep running. During an outage, the battery can use its entire stored charge, including the reserve percentage it normally holds back, down to a small backup floor that protects the battery. When grid power returns, the battery reconnects on its own and goes back to your chosen operating mode.

chunks.title: Backup Power During Outages
chunks.heading: How long backup lasts
chunks.text: How long your battery can power your home in an outage depends on how much charge it has, its capacity, and how much power your home is using. A good estimate is: hours of backup ≈ (state of charge % − backup floor %) × capacity in kWh ÷ your home's load in kW. The backup floor is 5% for the VoltNest 13 and 10% for the Helio PowerCell 10; your battery's manual lists it. For example, a VoltNest 13 (13.5 kWh) at 42% charge with the home using 1.2 kW holds about (0.37 × 13.5) ≈ 5.0 usable kWh, which lasts about 4.2 hours.

chunks.title: Backup Power During Outages
chunks.heading: Stretching backup time
chunks.text: You can make your battery last longer during an outage by lowering your home's load. Turn off the largest users first: air conditioning, electric ovens and stoves, clothes dryers, pool pumps, and electric vehicle chargers. Cutting the load in half roughly doubles the backup time. During daylight, rooftop solar keeps recharging the battery during an outage, so a sunny day can extend backup well beyond the estimate from the battery's charge alone.

chunks.title: Backup Power During Outages
chunks.heading: Preparing for a storm
chunks.text: If a storm or planned outage is coming, prepare your battery the day before. Switch it to its outage-saving mode, which keeps it full for the outage, or raise the reserve percentage to 80% or higher in the app. On a VoltNest 13 that mode is called Backup Only; on a Helio PowerCell 10 it is called Storm Guard. Charge the battery fully if you can, using solar during the day or the grid overnight. After the storm passes, switch back to your usual mode.

chunks.title: Backup Power During Outages
chunks.heading: What backup can't power
chunks.text: Your battery can only supply so much power at once: up to 5.0 kW for a VoltNest 13 and 3.8 kW for a Helio PowerCell 10. During an outage it cannot run large loads that add up to more than that, such as central air conditioning together with an electric oven and dryer. It also only powers circuits connected to the backup panel; anything wired outside it goes dark in an outage. Changing which circuits are backed up requires work in the electrical panel and must be done by a licensed electrician.

chunks.title: Your Rooftop Solar System
chunks.heading: System size
chunks.text: Your rooftop solar system is rated at 7.2 kW. It is made up of eighteen 400 W panels on the roof, connected to an inverter that turns the panels' power into electricity your home can use. The 7.2 kW rating is the most the system can produce at one moment in ideal conditions. In practice, it produces less than that most of the time, depending on the time of day, the season, and the weather.

chunks.title: Your Rooftop Solar System
chunks.heading: A typical day's production
chunks.text: On a sunny day, the 7.2 kW rooftop solar system produces about 35 kWh in total. Production starts around 6 AM, climbs through the morning, and peaks around noon at about 5 kWh per hour. It then falls through the afternoon and ends around 7 PM. Most of the day's energy arrives between 9 AM and 4 PM. That midday surplus is what charges your battery for the evening, when the 4 PM to 9 PM peak prices begin.

chunks.title: Your Rooftop Solar System
chunks.heading: Cloudy days
chunks.text: On a cloudy day, the rooftop solar system produces roughly a third of what it makes on a sunny day, around 10 kWh instead of 35 kWh, with a midday peak of about 1.5 kWh per hour. That is often not enough to cover the home's daytime use and fill the battery. A low solar forecast for tomorrow is the main reason to charge the battery from the grid overnight, during the cheapest hours.

chunks.title: Your Rooftop Solar System
chunks.heading: How solar and the battery work together
chunks.text: Your rooftop solar system and home battery share the work in a set order. Solar power goes first to whatever your home is using right now. Any extra solar then charges the battery. Once the battery is full, the rest is exported to the grid for a credit. In the evening, when solar production stops, the battery powers your home with the energy it stored during the day, which keeps you from buying power at peak prices.

chunks.title: Your Rooftop Solar System
chunks.heading: Keeping panels productive
chunks.text: Rooftop solar panels need very little care. Dust and pollen can lower production by a few percent, and rain usually washes the panels clean on its own. If production looks much lower than usual on a sunny day, check the inverter for warning lights in the app. Never climb onto the roof to clean or inspect the panels yourself. Any work on the panels, roof wiring, or inverter must be done by a licensed electrician or a certified solar technician.

chunks.title: Brightline Energy Sunrise Saver Plan
chunks.heading: How time-of-use pricing works
chunks.text: The Sunrise Saver plan from Brightline Energy is a time-of-use plan: the price you pay for each kWh of electricity depends on the time of day you use it. Power is cheapest overnight, when demand on the grid is low, and most expensive in the late afternoon and evening, when everyone gets home and turns things on. You save money on the Sunrise Saver plan by shifting energy use away from peak hours, either by running appliances at cheaper times or by letting a home battery cover the expensive hours.

chunks.title: Brightline Energy Sunrise Saver Plan
chunks.heading: Rate periods and prices
chunks.text: The Sunrise Saver plan has four rate periods each day. Super off-peak runs from 12 AM to 6 AM at $0.11 per kWh, the cheapest time to use or store power. Off-peak runs from 6 AM to 4 PM at $0.24 per kWh. Peak runs from 4 PM to 9 PM at $0.48 per kWh, the most expensive time of day. Off-peak returns from 9 PM to 12 AM at $0.24 per kWh. Peak power costs more than four times as much as super off-peak power, so moving even a few kWh out of the 4 PM to 9 PM window makes a noticeable difference.

chunks.title: Brightline Energy Sunrise Saver Plan
chunks.heading: Weekends and holidays
chunks.text: On the Sunrise Saver plan, the same rate periods and prices apply every day of the year, including weekends and public holidays. There is no separate weekend schedule: 12 AM to 6 AM is always super off-peak at $0.11 per kWh, and 4 PM to 9 PM is always peak at $0.48 per kWh. This makes the plan easy to plan around, because the cheapest and most expensive hours never move.

chunks.title: Brightline Energy Sunrise Saver Plan
chunks.heading: Solar export credit
chunks.text: When your rooftop solar produces more than your home and battery can use, the extra energy flows back to the grid. On the Sunrise Saver plan, Brightline Energy credits exported solar at $0.07 per kWh. That credit is lower than every purchase price on the plan, including the $0.11 super off-peak rate. Storing extra solar in your battery and using it during peak hours is usually worth far more than exporting it, because each stored kWh can replace power that would cost $0.48 per kWh.

chunks.title: Brightline Energy Sunrise Saver Plan
chunks.heading: Fixed monthly charge
chunks.text: The Sunrise Saver plan includes a fixed service charge of $12.00 per month. Brightline Energy charges this amount whether you use a lot of electricity or very little, and it does not change with time-of-use periods. Everything else on your bill comes from the energy you buy at each period's price, minus any credit for solar you export.

chunks.title: Brightline Energy Sunrise Saver Plan
chunks.heading: Tips to save on this plan
chunks.text: To save on the Sunrise Saver plan, run large appliances such as the dishwasher, washing machine, and dryer before 4 PM or after 9 PM. Charge an electric vehicle between 12 AM and 6 AM, when power costs $0.11 per kWh. Let your home battery cover your home's use during the 4 PM to 9 PM peak. Pre-cool your home in the early afternoon on hot days so the air conditioner works less during peak hours.
